content.text:
I found one claim the record contradicts. The rest of the document's claims are supported.

**Flagged: causal chain 2.** It says the calls to io-pricing took about 1500ms "for most of the requests sampled each minute." The slow-call log line (G9feb) usually counts 200 of 200 requests, but in at least one minute it counts only 88 of 200. That's fewer than half, so "most … each minute" doesn't hold for every minute.

**Supported, with notes on the close calls:**
- **Root cause and the plain-words cause:** Both rest on Code-Fix's reading (F1) and the call site Argus read (U1), and both are hedged. One says "in the files Code-Fix read" and "unverified", the other "likely".
- **Causal chain 3:** The "no time limit" part comes from Code-Fix's reading, not from a test, but the field cites F1 and U1 and the root cause already says it is unverified. So I didn't flag it.
- **Contributing factor 3:** It doesn't name Code-Fix as its source, but it repeats F1's own description of the existing tests. I accepted it on that basis.
- **Contributing factor 2:** "No alert on io-pricing" is fine because the record holds none.
- **"Got lucky":** Only its facts were judged: the restart came at 02:28:12, the service was back by 02:29, and the fault lasted 8 minutes.

The action items and the what-if halves of the contributing factors weren't judged.

flags.quote: for most of the requests sampled each minute
flags.why: The slow-call log line (G9feb) counts 88 to 200 slow requests out of 200 per minute, so at least one minute had fewer than half, not most.

supported.quote: In the files Code-Fix read, io-shop's account page gets the basket total by calling io-pricing inline through `basket_total`, which waits however long the call takes and sets no time limit.

The page already falls back to rendering without the total when the call raises `PricingServiceFailed`, but a slow call never raises, so however long io-pricing took was added straight onto the account page's response time. It rests on F1, a reading of the source nothing ran, so it is unverified.

The shop's account page waits for a separate pricing service to work out the shopper's basket total, and it likely has no time limit on that wait, so when the pricing service slowed down the page slowed down too, even though it could have been shown without the total.
io-pricing could slow down again, and io-shop's account pages could slow down with it.
Shop pages loaded slowly for shoppers

Shoppers waited longer for io-shop's pages: the slowest requests, the ones the service's high-percentile response time tracks, took far longer than before, while failed requests stayed within their normal range.
io-shop was waiting on io-pricing: from the onset, its calls to io-pricing for a shopper's basket total took about {G9feb.1} each
A slow io-pricing answer slowed the page because the account page calls `basket_total` inline and waits for the basket total with no time limit.
The HighLatency alert on io-shop paged nobody: no on-call incident was linked to it.
rows: Nobody was paged: no on-call incident was linked to this one

supported.quote: The record shows no alert on io-pricing's own latency. The slowdown was found only by io-shop's latency alert and then worked out from io-shop's slow-upstream-call log lines.
io-shop's existing tests of the pricing call use fakes that answer straight away and only report a large `took_ms`, so the tests never exercised a pricing service that actually hangs.
Argus restarted io-pricing without knowing why it had slowed down, and the restart still brought the service back, which kept the slowdown short.
